To prove the theorem `lg_target`, we aim to show that for any real number $ x $, and given $ p \geq 0 $ and $ t \neq 0 $, the inequality $ |x|^p \leq \left(\frac{p}{|t|}\right)^p \cdot \max\left(e^{tx}, e^{-tx}\right) $ holds.

The key idea is to recognize that $ \max(e^{tx}, e^{-tx}) = e^{|t||x|} $. So the right-hand side simplifies to $ \left(\frac{p}{|t|}\right)^p \cdot e^{|t||x|} $. This transforms the inequality into:

$$
|x|^p \leq \left(\frac{p}{|t|}\right)^p \cdot e^{|t||x|}
$$

Taking both sides to the power $ 1/p $, we get:

$$
|x| \leq \frac{p}{|t|} \cdot e^{|t||x|^{1/p}}
$$

This is a standard inequality involving exponential functions and can be proven using the convexity of the exponential function or by applying the AM-GM inequality in combination with properties of exponentials. The final step involves verifying the inequality under the given assumptions and using appropriate inequalities from Mathlib, such as bounds on exponentials or properties of maxima.
